concepts_used: Article 19(1)(g): Freedom to Practice Any Profession or Carry on Any Occupation, Trade or Business

solution.concept_anchor: Article 19(1)(g) — illegal or harmful activities excluded
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students may identify lottery operations as morally questionable and select it as the odd one out, not realising that State-run lotteries are a legitimate regulated trade while underground gambling is what falls outside 19(1)(g) protection.
elimination_logic: Identify what the three similar items share: they are all activities that have been recognised as falling within the protection of Article 19(1)(g) as legitimate trades/professions subject to regulation.
Lottery ticket sales (State-regulated): regulated trade, falls within 19(1)(g).
Legal practice (advocacy): a profession requiring qualifications, falls within 19(1)(g).
Liquor trade (licensed): licensed, restricted, but still a trade within 19(1)(g) (some courts go further to say it is res extra commercium, but it is at minimum regulated under 19(1)(g)).
Running an underground gambling den: this is an illegal activity — Article 19(1)(g) does not protect illegal or criminally prohibited activities.
Option (a) — underground gambling — is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) — liquor trade — is the most tempting wrong answer because liquor is morally contentious and some judicial opinions have characterised it as res extra commercium. However, it remains a licensed, regulated trade under 19(1)(g). Underground gambling is illegal and therefore outside Article 19(1)(g) protection entirely — illegal activities cannot claim fundamental right protection.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 19(1)(g) protects the right to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade, or business — but this protection expressly does not extend to activities that are illegal, immoral, or inherently harmful in a manner that places them outside the realm of legitimate trade.

• Option (a): Underground gambling — the odd one out. It is a criminal activity under gambling laws and cannot claim fundamental right protection under 19(1)(g).
• Option (b): Legal practice (advocacy) — a profession requiring Bar Council qualification; clearly within 19(1)(g).
• Option (c): Licensed liquor trade — while heavily regulated (and some courts have called it res extra commercium), it remains a licensed activity within 19(1)(g)'s ambit.
• Option (d): State-regulated lottery ticket sales — a lawful regulated business activity protected under 19(1)(g).

Value Addition:
• Immoral trafficking, drug trade, and prostitution are similarly outside 19(1)(g) protection.
• The concept of 'res extra commercium' places certain activities (e.g., prostitution, some interpretations of liquor) entirely outside commerce, disentitling them from fundamental rights protection.
• Begging has been held by some High Courts to fall within the scope of 19(1)(g) as a livelihood.

solution.concept_anchor: Landmark press and speech cases matched to principles
solution.strong_distractor: b — Swapping Romesh Thappar (public order vs law and order) with Sakal Papers (price-page schedule) is the core entity-swap trap since both cases involve restrictions on newspapers and both were decided in the early 1950s–1960s.
elimination_logic: Anchor on List II item 1 (Bijoe Emmanuel — right to remain silent): this is a well-known holding, matches List I item C.
Anchor on List II item 4 (Sakal Papers — newspaper pricing regulation struck down): matches List I item B — price-page schedule was the Sakal Papers holding.
Romesh Thappar (List I item A) is known for public order vs law and order distinction — matches List II item 2.
Tata Press (List I item D) is known for commercial speech protection — matches List II item 3.
Full matching: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 — correct answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Romesh Thappar and Sakal Papers are both press freedom cases decided in the same era, both involving newspaper regulations. Students who recall both as 'struck down newspaper restrictions' may swap their specific holdings. Romesh Thappar's primary holding is the public order/law and order distinction; Sakal Papers is about price-page schedules being indirect restrictions.
solution.final_explanation:
Each of these cases established a distinct and lasting constitutional principle under Article 19.

• A-2: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras — established the distinction between 'public order' (wide) and 'law and order' (narrow); a restriction justified only on law and order grounds cannot satisfy the 19(2) public order ground.
• B-4: Sakal Papers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India — the newspaper price-page schedule imposed by the government indirectly restricted press freedom by controlling circulation; the Court struck it down.
• C-1: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala — established the right to remain silent as the negative dimension of Article 19(1)(a); expulsion of children who would not sing the national anthem was unconstitutional.
• D-3: Tata Press Ltd. v. MTNL — commercial speech (advertising) is protected under Article 19(1)(a); the listener's right to receive information is part of free speech.

Correct matching: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3.

Value Addition:
• All four cases are frequently tested in combination — memorise each by its specific holding, not merely its subject area.
• Romesh Thappar (1950) prompted the 1st Constitutional Amendment (1951) adding public order and friendly relations with foreign states to 19(2).
• Tata Press extended free speech protection to commercial actors for the first time.

solution.concept_anchor: Arbitrary qualifications as unreasonable restrictions under 19(1)(g)
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may choose option (b), believing that once the State has the express power under 19(6) to prescribe qualifications, any qualification it prescribes is automatically reasonable — not appreciating that arbitrariness or excessive requirements remain subject to judicial review.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): the State cannot prescribe qualifications for any professional activity without limitation — only where relevant to protect public interest.
Eliminate option (b): the power to prescribe qualifications under 19(6) does not confer absolute immunity from judicial review; the qualifications must still be reasonable.
Eliminate option (c): professional qualifications are specifically mentioned in 19(6) — they are a ground for restriction, not a violation of 19(1)(g).

Option (d) is correct: while the State has the power to prescribe professional qualifications, qualifications that are arbitrary, excessive, or have no rational connection to the professional objective are unreasonable restrictions and can be struck down by courts.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) exploits the student's correct knowledge that Article 19(6) expressly authorises professional qualification requirements. The trap is in concluding that express authorisation equals automatic reasonableness — courts retain the power to invalidate qualifications that are arbitrary, excessive, or bear no rational nexus to the profession's requirements.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 19(6) expressly permits the State to prescribe professional or technical qualifications for any profession, occupation, trade, or business. However, this power is not unlimited.

• Option (a): Incorrect — the State can prescribe qualifications only where relevant to protect public interest and professional integrity; blanket qualification powers for any activity are not permitted.
• Option (b): Incorrect — the existence of express power under 19(6) does not immunise all qualifications from judicial scrutiny. Reasonableness still applies.
• Option (c): Incorrect — professional qualifications are an expressly permitted ground under 19(6); per se they do not violate 19(1)(g).
• Option (d): Correct — qualifications that are arbitrary, bear no rational connection to the professional task, or are excessive in nature go beyond 'reasonable restriction' and can be invalidated by courts as violating Article 19(1)(g).

Value Addition:
• The Bar Council of India regulates legal qualifications; Medical Council of India (now NMC) regulates medical qualifications — both derive authority from statutory and 19(6) frameworks.
• A qualification requirement designed to exclude competition rather than ensure competence is per se unreasonable.
• The proportionality doctrine applies to qualification requirements — they must be necessary and not merely convenient.

solution.concept_anchor: Constitutional amendments expanding Article 19(2) grounds
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know the 16th Amendment added sovereignty and integrity but are unsure whether it came before or after the 1st Amendment (which added public order and friendly relations) may swap the two, making option (c) appealing.
elimination_logic: Anchor the Constitution's original enactment: 1950 — original Article 19(2) had four grounds (security of state, friendly relations with foreign states, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation — note: original wording was limited).

First Amendment (1951): added 'sovereignty and integrity' and 'friendly relations with foreign states' as express grounds; also introduced 'public order' — enacted AFTER Romesh Thappar exposed limitations.
Sixteenth Amendment (1963): specifically added 'sovereignty and integrity of India' as a ground across Articles 19(2), (3), and (4) — primarily in response to separatist movements.
Correct chronological order: Constitution enacted (1950) → 1st Amendment (1951) → 16th Amendment (1963) — answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 1st Amendment and 16th Amendment both deal with sovereignty/integrity and public order, making temporal confusion easy. The 1st Amendment is famous for multiple reasons (9th Schedule, Article 31A), so students may not specifically associate it with expanding Article 19(2) grounds. The 16th Amendment's narrower focus on sovereignty/integrity makes it easy to over-date or under-date.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 19(2) has been amended twice to expand its grounds. The original Constitution's Article 19(2) had grounds including security of state and public order, but the Supreme Court's ruling in Romesh Thappar exposed that the existing grounds were insufficient to cover certain restrictions Parliament wished to impose.

First Constitutional Amendment (1951): Expanded 19(2) to expressly include public order, friendly relations with foreign states, and incitement to offence — directly addressing the Romesh Thappar gap.

Sixteenth Constitutional Amendment (1963): Added 'sovereignty and integrity of India' as a ground across Articles 19(2), (3), and (4) — enacted in the context of separatist agitation and to enable restrictions on speech/assembly/associations challenging India's territorial integrity.

Correct order: Original Constitution (1950) → 1st Amendment (1951) → 16th Amendment (1963) — answer is (b).

Value Addition:
• The 9th Schedule was also introduced by the 1st Amendment — making it one of the most consequential amendments to the Constitution.
• The 16th Amendment also inserted oath requirements for legislators regarding sovereignty/integrity.
• The 44th Amendment (1978) is associated with emergency provisions, not Article 19(2).

solution.concept_anchor: Modern Dental College — four-fold proportionality test
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who associate proportionality with the Puttaswamy privacy case (which extensively discussed proportionality) may select (b), not realising that Puttaswamy applied proportionality to Article 21, while Modern Dental College applied it specifically to Article 19 restrictions.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (d): Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) expanded the scope of Article 21 and introduced the fairness test but did not formally apply the four-fold proportionality doctrine to Article 19.
Eliminate option (c): Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) struck down Section 66A IT Act but focused on the 'public order' nexus and overbreadth — not the four-fold proportionality framework.
Eliminate option (b): Puttaswamy applied proportionality to privacy under Article 21; it is not the case that formally introduced the four-fold proportionality test for Article 19 restrictions.

Option (a) Modern Dental College & Research Centre v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2016) is the case that formally adopted the four-fold proportionality framework (legitimate goal, rational connection, necessity, balancing) for Article 19 restrictions — correct answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Puttaswamy is the most high-profile case on proportionality in Indian constitutional law, leading many students to attribute all proportionality doctrine to it. The more targeted application of the four-fold proportionality test to Article 19 restrictions specifically was in Modern Dental College — a less celebrated but equally important case.
solution.final_explanation:
The four-fold proportionality test — (i) legitimate aim, (ii) rational nexus, (iii) necessity/least restrictive means, and (iv) fair balance — was formally adopted for evaluating restrictions on Article 19 rights in the case of Modern Dental College & Research Centre v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2016), where the Supreme Court applied this framework to examine the constitutional validity of restrictions on private medical colleges' rights under Article 19(1)(g).

• Option (a): Correct — Modern Dental College formally embedded the four-fold proportionality test in Article 19 analysis.
• Option (b): Incorrect — Puttaswamy applied proportionality to the right to privacy under Article 21; it did not originate the four-fold test for Article 19.
• Option (c): Incorrect — Shreya Singhal focused on overbreadth and the nexus between speech and public order disruption, not the formal proportionality framework.
• Option (d): Incorrect — Maneka Gandhi introduced procedural fairness for Article 21, not the proportionality test for Article 19.

Value Addition:
• The four-fold test is the modern evolution from the older 'reasonable restriction' standard.
• The 'necessity' limb requires the State to use the least rights-restrictive measure available.
• Proportionality is now applied across Articles 19, 21, and 14 in Indian constitutional jurisprudence.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 356 vs 358 — which emergencies affect Article 19

statement_analysis.statement: Article 19 rights are automatically suspended when President's Rule is imposed under Article 356 in a State.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 358 provides for suspension of Article 19 only during a National Emergency under Article 352. President's Rule (Article 356) does not suspend Article 19 rights — it only transfers State executive and legislative powers to the Centre.

statement_analysis.statement: During a Financial Emergency under Article 360, Article 19 rights of citizens are suspended by operation of Article 358.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 358 applies only to National Emergency proclaimed under Article 352 on grounds of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion. Financial Emergency (Article 360) does not suspend Article 19 rights.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 359, the President can issue an order suspending the right of citizens to move courts for enforcement of all fundamental rights, including Articles 20 and 21, during a National Emergency.
statement_analysis.reason: The 44th Amendment specifically excluded Articles 20 and 21 from the scope of Article 359 — the President cannot suspend the enforcement of these two rights even during a National Emergency through an Article 359 order.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may believe that at least Statement 2 contains some truth (emergencies do restrict rights in various ways), making 'only Statement 2 is not correct' tempting; but Statement 2 is wholly incorrect — Financial Emergency does not suspend Article 19.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: President's Rule (356) does not trigger Article 358's automatic suspension of 19 — only National Emergency (352) does. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Statement 2: Financial Emergency (360) has no provision for suspending Article 19 — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3: Post-44th Amendment, Articles 20 and 21 are immune from Article 359 orders — Statement 3 is incorrect.
All three statements are not correct — answer is (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges the three types of emergencies (National, State/President's Rule, Financial) and incorrectly attributes Article 19 suspension powers to all three. In reality, only National Emergency under Article 352 triggers Article 358. This is one of the most tested emergency-fundamental rights interactions in UPSC.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between emergency provisions and Article 19 is precisely delineated in the Constitution.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: President's Rule (Article 356) does not suspend Article 19. It transfers the governance of a State to the Centre but leaves fundamental rights intact. Article 358 operates exclusively during National Emergency under Article 352.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Financial Emergency (Article 360) has no provision for suspending fundamental rights including Article 19. It only empowers the Centre to direct the financial management of states.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) inserted an express exception in Article 359 — Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even by a Presidential Order under 359 during a National Emergency.

All three statements are incorrect — answer is (d).

Value Addition:
• Article 358 operates automatically upon National Emergency proclamation — no additional order needed.
• Article 359 requires a specific Presidential Order identifying which rights' enforcement is suspended.
• The distinction between Article 358 (Article 19 specific) and Article 359 (other rights, order required) is frequently tested.

solution.concept_anchor: Aadhaar case — balancing privacy with right to livelihood

statement_analysis.statement: In the Aadhaar case, the Supreme Court held that mandatory linking of Aadhaar with welfare schemes violates the right to privacy under Article 21 but that the Aadhaar Act itself is constitutionally valid.
statement_analysis.reason: The majority in the Aadhaar case (Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India — Aadhaar) upheld the Aadhaar Act as constitutionally valid but struck down certain provisions, including mandatory Aadhaar-PAN linking for non-government purposes and mandatory Aadhaar for bank accounts and mobile numbers. The core holding balanced privacy with the State's interest in efficient welfare delivery.

statement_analysis.statement: The Aadhaar case held that the mandatory requirement of Aadhaar for welfare benefits violates Article 19(1)(g), since the inability to access livelihood-linked schemes without biometric authentication amounts to an unreasonable restriction on the right to earn a living.
statement_analysis.reason: The Aadhaar case did not hold that mandatory Aadhaar for government welfare schemes violates Article 19(1)(g). The majority upheld Aadhaar-based authentication for government schemes as a constitutionally valid condition, reasoning that the right to livelihood under 19(1)(g) does not include an unconditional right to government benefits on one's own terms.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the Aadhaar judgment involved both privacy and livelihood may accept both statements as broadly describing the judgment, not catching that Statement 2 over-extends the ruling into a 19(1)(g) violation finding that the Court did not actually make.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: The Aadhaar Act was upheld as a whole by the majority; specific provisions (private entity use, mandatory bank-mobile linking) were struck down. The broad description in Statement 1 is substantially accurate — mark correct.
Verify Statement 2: The Court did not hold that mandatory Aadhaar for government welfare violates 19(1)(g). The majority upheld Aadhaar for welfare schemes. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 extends the actual holding of the Aadhaar case into a domain the Court did not reach. The Court upheld Aadhaar for government welfare delivery and did not find a violation of Article 19(1)(g) in that context. Students who recall 'Aadhaar-privacy-livelihood' as linked concepts may accept Statement 2 without checking whether the 19(1)(g) violation was actually held.
solution.final_explanation:
The Aadhaar case (Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India — 2018) involved a comprehensive challenge to the Aadhaar Act on grounds of privacy and fundamental rights. The majority upheld the Aadhaar Act as constitutional but struck down specific provisions that permitted private entities to use Aadhaar authentication and that mandated Aadhaar linking for private services.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Aadhaar Act was upheld as valid; certain provisions were struck down as disproportionate privacy violations. The core scheme for government welfare delivery was upheld.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Court did not hold that mandatory Aadhaar for welfare schemes violates Article 19(1)(g). The majority found the welfare delivery mechanism constitutionally valid — the right to livelihood does not entitle a person to access government benefits on their own authentication terms.

Value Addition:
• The Aadhaar case has multiple opinions (majority, concurring, dissenting) — the dissent (Justice D.Y. Chandrachud) found the entire Act unconstitutional as a money bill and on privacy grounds.
• Aadhaar-PAN mandatory linking for income tax was upheld; for bank accounts and mobiles it was struck down.
• The case demonstrated the intersection of Articles 14, 19, and 21 in privacy-livelihood balancing.

solution.concept_anchor: Proportionality — restriction on assembly must be least restrictive means
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know the State can restrict assembly in sensitive areas for public order may select (c), not recognising that a blanket prohibition on all assembly within an entire city for three weeks fails the proportionality and least-restrictive-means test.
elimination_logic: Identify the applicable principles: Article 19(1)(b) protects peaceful assembly; restrictions under 19(3) must be on grounds of public order and must satisfy proportionality.

Apply the proportionality test: (i) legitimate aim — yes, public order is valid; (ii) rational nexus — a prohibition within the entire city for three weeks is disproportionately wide; (iii) necessity/least restrictive means — targeted restrictions around specific sensitive locations would be sufficient; (iv) balancing — three weeks of blanket prohibition is excessive.
Eliminate option (a): the right to assemble can be restricted — the scenario does not make the restriction per se unconstitutional solely because it cites public order.
Eliminate option (c): Section 144 is a valid tool but a three-week blanket citywide prohibition fails proportionality.
Eliminate option (d): judicial review is not suspended during public order emergencies.

Option (b) correctly identifies that while public order is a valid ground, the scope and duration of the blanket prohibition fail proportionality — courts would require targeted, time-limited measures.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap lies in option (c): Section 144 CrPC has been upheld as constitutionally valid, but this does not mean every Section 144 order is immune from review. The proportionality doctrine requires that even valid legal mechanisms be applied in a proportionate manner — citywide three-week blanket prohibitions are disproportionate even when the underlying ground (public order) is valid.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the application of the proportionality doctrine to assembly restrictions. The right to assemble peaceably under Article 19(1)(b) is subject to restrictions on grounds of public order (Article 19(3)), but any such restriction must satisfy the proportionality test — it must be the least restrictive means necessary to achieve the public order objective.

A blanket prohibition on all assembly anywhere within an entire city for three weeks fails proportionality on multiple counts: (i) it is geographically overbroad — targeted restrictions near sensitive areas would suffice; (ii) it is temporally excessive — three weeks without review is indefinite in practical effect; and (iii) the balancing test favours a targeted approach over wholesale suppression of assembly rights.

• Option (a): Incorrect — public order is a valid ground, but the manner of restriction can still be challenged.
• Option (b): Correct — public order is a valid ground, but blanket citywide prohibition for three weeks is disproportionate; courts would require targeted, time-bound, periodically reviewed restrictions.
• Option (c): Incorrect — Section 144's constitutional validity does not immunise every order made under it from proportionality review.
• Option (d): Incorrect — courts retain full power of judicial review; public order situations do not suspend judicial oversight.

Value Addition:
• Section 144 orders must specify the threat and the geographic and temporal limits — open-ended orders are constitutionally suspect.
• Anuradha Bhasin's proportionality principles for internet shutdowns apply analogously to assembly restrictions.
• Periodic review of continuing restrictions is now a constitutional requirement across restriction domains.

solution.concept_anchor: Exclusions from 19(1)(a) — hate speech, defamation, contempt

statement_analysis.statement: Defamation is constitutionally recognised as a ground for restricting freedom of speech under Article 19(2) and criminal defamation laws have been upheld by the Supreme Court as valid restrictions.
statement_analysis.reason: Defamation is one of the eight express grounds in Article 19(2). Criminal defamation under Sections 499-500 IPC was upheld as a constitutionally valid reasonable restriction in Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016).

statement_analysis.statement: Hate speech directed against a religious community falls under the 'incitement to offence' ground in Article 19(2) and can never be protected under Article 19(1)(a).
statement_analysis.reason: The claim that hate speech can 'never' be protected is too absolute. The constitutional position requires that restrictions on speech — including hate speech — must satisfy the direct and proximate nexus test with a permissible ground; not all hate speech automatically falls within Article 19(2) grounds without that nexus. Additionally, 'incitement to offence' requires a nexus to an actual or likely offence.

statement_analysis.statement: Contempt of court is both a restriction ground under Article 19(2) and a free-standing power of courts under Article 129 (Supreme Court) and Article 215 (High Courts).
statement_analysis.reason: Contempt of court appears as a ground in Article 19(2) AND as an independent constitutional power of courts under Articles 129 and 215 — the two operate on separate legal planes.

statement_analysis.statement: The right to silence and the right to remain anonymous are both explicitly mentioned as components of the freedom of speech and expression in the constitutional text of Article 19(1)(a).
statement_analysis.reason: Neither the right to silence nor the right to remain anonymous is explicitly mentioned in Article 19(1)(a) — they have been judicially derived from the freedom of speech and expression through interpretation (Bijoe Emmanuel for right to silence). The constitutional text contains no such explicit mention.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students may accept Statement 2 as broadly correct (hate speech is generally restricted) without catching the absolute qualifier 'never' that makes it constitutionally overstated.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — defamation is an express ground; criminal defamation upheld in Subramanian Swamy.
Statement 2 is incorrect — the word 'never' makes it false; constitutional restrictions require direct nexus; not all hate speech auto-qualifies.
Statement 3 is correct — contempt of court exists in both 19(2) and independently under Articles 129/215.
Statement 4 is incorrect — right to silence and anonymity are judicially derived, not explicitly mentioned in constitutional text.
Two statements (1 and 3) are correct — answer is (b) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses 'never,' which is a scope-extension trap — students who know hate speech can be restricted may overlook that the absolute qualifier over-states the constitutional position. Statement 4 exploits imprecise memory about constitutional text versus judicial interpretation.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 19(1)(a)'s scope and the grounds for restricting it under 19(2) involve several precision-sensitive facts.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Defamation is express in 19(2); criminal defamation was upheld in Subramanian Swamy (2016).
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: 'Never' is constitutionally untenable. Restrictions must satisfy the nexus test with a permissible ground — not all hate speech automatically satisfies this. The qualifier makes the statement false.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Contempt of court operates on two levels — as an Article 19(2) restriction ground AND as an independent power under Articles 129 and 215.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Right to silence (Bijoe Emmanuel) and right to anonymity are judicially derived expansions of 19(1)(a) — they are not in the constitutional text.

Two statements correct — answer is (b).

Value Addition:
• Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016) is the leading case on criminal defamation's constitutional validity.
• The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 operationalises the contempt ground under 19(2).
• Anonymous speech (e.g., pseudonymous writing) may have constitutional protection as part of 19(1)(a) in appropriate contexts.

solution.concept_anchor: Inner Line Permit, tribal restrictions — valid 19(5) measures
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may swap List I item C (Inner Line Permit states) with a different set of northeastern states, particularly including Meghalaya and excluding Nagaland or Arunachal Pradesh.
elimination_logic: Anchor on List I item A (Article 19(1)(d)): the right to move freely is temporary/transit movement — matches with List II item 3 (temporary movement throughout territory).
Anchor on List I item B (Article 19(1)(e)): reside and settle is permanent establishment — matches with List II item 1 (permanent residence and settlement).

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Inner Line Permit states are a precision geography trap. Meghalaya is frequently but wrongly included in ILP states by students. The correct states are Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Mizoram, and Manipur (since December 2019). Option (b) introduces Meghalaya as a swap for one of the correct states.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 19(1)(d) and 19(1)(e) protect distinct aspects of territorial rights, and Article 19(5) provides their shared restriction clause.

• A-3: Article 19(1)(d) — freedom to move freely throughout India — covers temporary movement, travel, and transit. It does not confer a right to permanently settle.
• B-1: Article 19(1)(e) — freedom to reside and settle — covers permanent or long-term residence and the right to establish one's domicile anywhere in India.
• C-4: The Inner Line Permit system currently applies to Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Mizoram, and Manipur (added 2019) — not Meghalaya. It requires non-residents of these states to obtain permits before entering.
• D-2: Article 19(5) is the shared restriction clause for both 19(1)(d) and 19(1)(e) — it permits restrictions in the interests of the general public OR for protection of Scheduled Tribes.

Correct matching: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 — answer is (d).

Value Addition:
• Protected Area Permits operate near international borders and are distinct from Inner Line Permits.
• Nagaland has both ILP restrictions and special protections under Article 371A.
• The Chin-Lushai Hill tracts provision in Mizoram also intersects with 19(5) restrictions.
